Riyadh rolls over $3bn as prospects of $10bn US facility wane. • Aurangzeb says proposed US facility is not essential, would provide additional support if secured • Further Eurobond, Panda bond and rupee-linked dollar-settled issuances planned • Govt targets $4bn reduction in external debt ISLAMABAD: Pakistan has secured a $3 billion rollover from Saudi Arabia, as prospects of a proposed $10bn US backstop facility appear to have waned, it emerged on Wednesday. Speaking to journalists at Parliament House, Finance Minister Muhammad Auran­gzeb confirmed that Riyadh had extended the $3bn financing it provided in April this year to bridge a gap arising from $3.5bn in repayments to the United Arab Emirates. “It has been extended and for a reasonable period. You don’t need to worry as to for how long given the kind of strategic relationship we have,” he said when asked about the facility, which matured on Oct 31 under its three-month term. He said he had a very good meeting with his Saudi counterpart, Mohammed Al-Jadaan, during the recent World Bank-IMF meetings in Bangkok. Saudi Arabia had already extended its $5bn facility until 2028. Asked whether Pakistan had also sought additional support, the minister categorically denied it, saying this was not needed as foreign exchange reserves covered more than three months of imports and would be strengthened to provide a four-month import cover by the end of the year through capital markets. Responding to another question about the prospects of the $10bn Exchange Stabilisation Support Facility (ESSF) requested from the US in July this year, he sought to lower expectations that he himself had raised over the past several months. “What we asked for back in July and were looking at was the market access. We have got the market access,” he said, referring to the $3bn bond Pakistan issued in September against orders worth $6bn. “If that (ESSF) materialises, fantastic, it will be a liquidity support facility. Otherwise, we have plans for further Eurobond issuance, Panda bond issuance and rupee-linked dollar-settled bond,” the minister said. He added that he had held meetings with 70-80 institutional investors in Bangkok, who had a very clear view of Pakistan, and that offers were available for five-year and 10-year maturities, “because clearly we are looking beyond the [IMF] programme”. He said the government was looking at the US from a broader perspective, as the US Export-Import Bank and Development Finance Corporation (DFC) needed to support their investors and exporters in Pakistan. “That is real financing and real credit,” he said, adding that the ESSF request was for a liquidity support facility to help the sovereign. “If possible, fine; if not, we are going to move forward, with or without it.” The finance minister also reported that the IMF Executive Board meeting to approve a disbursement of $1.2bn to Pakistan would be held in December. External debt Earlier, he told the Senate Standing Committee on Finance that Pakistan was targeting a reduction of $4bn in external debt during the current fiscal year and $3.5bn next year, compared with $4.5bn in the last fiscal year. He said the government was seeking to replace expensive short-term borrowing with longer-maturity financing through bonds and private placements to reduce refinancing risks. He said external debt had been rising by $5-6bn annually, from $45bn in 2014-15 to around $100bn, but had increased by only $1bn annually over the past two years. “Our objective is not to increase external debt. All the transactions like Eurobond, Panda bond or private placements have been replacement bonds to replace expensive with cheaper facilities,” he said, adding that fiscal discipline had helped contain the fiscal and current account deficits and, despite oil and wheat import bills, the current account deficit would be no more than 1pc this year. “This is hard-earned stability that helped create buffers to meet our requirements despite floods and war in the region, and foreign exchange reserves crossed $21.5bn, which is the best-ever level of reserves in our history,” he said, adding that Pakistan could not afford to lose this basic hygiene. Finance Secretary Imdadullah Bosal told the committee, which was presided over by Senator Saleem Mandviwalla, that public debt had declined to 68.6pc of GDP by the end of June 2026, from 75.1pc in fiscal year 2022-23. Year-on-year growth in public debt had slowed to 7.7pc in the last fiscal year, the lowest in 20 years, he said. The secretary said domestic debt amounted to Rs58.8 trillion by the end of August 2026, down from Rs68.4tr at the end of June, while foreign debt remained stable at $98.2bn. He reported net financing requirements of $11bn after rollovers and refinancing, of which $5bn had already been repaid in the first four months of the current fiscal year. The remaining $6bn was payable over the next seven months. The committee took strong exception to the difficulties faced by parliamentarians in obtaining foreign exchange for personal travel, saying the humiliation they faced at the hands of banks and the central bank was unacceptable. Mr Mandviwalla directed the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) to review existing procedures, including clearance requirements relating to politically exposed persons (PEPs) and the mandatory personal appearance of parliamentarians before exchange companies, despite their submission of valid passports, tickets and visas. The committee also expressed serious displeasure over the SBP’s response, dated Oct 30, 2026, to a letter sent by the committee secretary on its behalf to the SBP governor. It observed that the matter had been addressed by a deputy director-level officer instead of an appropriately senior authority. The chairman termed the requirement for personal appearance humiliating and called for an immediate review of the existing procedures, warning that the committee would take serious notice if the matter remained unresolved. UN panel hails Pakistan’s marriage-age law, flags bonded labour. • Experts seek details on child brides, rehabilitation of flood victims and reconstruction efforts • Pakistani delegation says 600,000 destroyed homes rebuilt ISLAMABAD: The United Nations Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights on Wednesday concluded its review of Pakistan’s second periodic report under the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, welcoming the country’s 2025 legal amendment raising the minimum age of marriage to 18. However, committee members raised questions about bonded labour and reconstruction efforts following the 2022 and 2025 floods, among other topics. Committee expert and member of the task force for Pakistan, Michael Windfuhr, welcomed the 2025 amendment to the Child Marriage Restraint Act 1929, which raised the minimum age of marriage to 18 for both males and females. However, he noted that the committee remained concerned about the high number of child brides and asked about the impact of measures taken to prevent child marriage. Lazhari Bouzid, another committee expert and member of the task force for Pakistan, said bonded labour continued to be prevalent in agriculture and was also found in the informal sector, particularly brick making. Construction companies and government agencies were reportedly complicit in the practice by purchasing bricks produced through debt bondage. He asked how Pakistan had responded to these reports. Mr Windfuhr also asked how the country had coped with the impact of the devastating floods in 2022 and 2025. He inquired whether Pakistan could rebuild housing for affected people and restore their access to land or resources, and how many people remained displaced. ‘Range of measures’ Minister of State for Law and Justice and head of the delegation, Barrister Aqeel Malik, said in his opening remarks that Pakistan had taken a range of legislative, policy and institutional measures since 2017 for the progressive realisation of covenant rights. He said child marriage restraint laws had set the minimum age of marriage at 18 for both boys and girls in Islamabad , Balochistan, Punjab and Sindh, and criminalised child, early and forced marriages. During the ensuing dialogue, the delegation said Pakistan’s Constitution prohibited slavery and all forms of forced labour, while the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1992 had abolished the practice. Punjab had documented more than 210,000 kiln workers, and district vigilance committees had been established in many districts. Labour inspectors had identified more than 2,900 victims of forced labour last year. On flood recovery, the delegation said the government had established a national emergency operations centre focusing on high-risk areas and launched a national flood protection programme. The programme aimed to protect at-risk people, eight million acres of agricultural land and 2.2 million housing units. Each province was also implementing flood protection measures. Of the 2.1 million homes destroyed in the 2022 floods, 600,000 had been rebuilt, while reconstruction of the remaining houses was under way. In her concluding remarks, committee expert and task force leader for Pakistan, Julieta Rossi, said the delegation had outlined processes for implementing economic, social and cultural rights, as well as the significant challenges facing the country and gaps between legislative progress and implementation. “This information would be reflected in the committee’s concluding observations, which the panel hoped that Pakistan would implement in good faith,” she added. Mr Malik said in his concluding remarks that the delegation had outlined its efforts to bridge the gaps between constitutional guarantees and their realisation. “The country’s trajectory was toward the progressive realisation of covenant rights,” he said, adding that despite constraints and challenges, Pakistan had made considerable progress since its first review. “[Pakistan] hopes that the committee’s candour and rigour will help pave the way for the full realisation of economic, social and cultural rights for all,” he added. Committee vice chair and acting chair of the dialogue, Asraf Ally Caunhye, thanked the delegation for its participation in the constructive dialogue and its expression of unwavering commitment to protecting the rights enshrined in the covenant. The Pakistani delegation comprised representatives from the Ministry of Law and Justice, the Ministry of Human Rights and the Permanent Mission of Pakistan to the United Nations Office at Geneva. Trump says Hegseth doing 'a very good job' as questions swirl about defence secretary's future. US President Donald Trump backed Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth a day after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in midterm elections that reflected voter anger over the war on Iran. Asked whether he was considering replacing Hegseth, whom he has described as a champion of the war, Trump told reporters: “No, I think he’s doing a very good job.” The response contrasted with then-president George Bush, who fired Defence Secretary Donald Rumsfeld the morning after the 2006 midterm elections, when voter discontent over the Iraq war helped Democrats win control of Congress. But sources said Trump could still replace Hegseth as Republicans assess their losses. One Trump adviser said Hegseth “could be on the chopping block” because of the war. “Someone is going to get blamed for this and you know it’s not going to be him (Trump),” the adviser said. Trump has described Hegseth as a key proponent of the unpopular conflict, saying on March 23: “Pete, I think you were the first one to speak up, and you said, ‘Let’s do it, because you can’t let them have a nuclear weapon.’” On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance publicly questioned whether the Iran war was worth it and said it cost Republicans control of Congress. Asked for comment, the White House referred Reuters to Trump’s public remarks on Hegseth. The Defence Department said Hegseth was “100 percent committed” to leading the Pentagon until the end of Trump’s term, which ends on Jan. 20, 2029. Impeachment threat Hegseth has been a polarising figure in American politics and has made adversaries even with his own Republican Party. One Republican lawmaker, US Representative Thomas Massie, even filed articles of impeachment against him earlier this year, accusing him of abusing his office by launching hostilities against Iran without approval by Congress. Republican US Senator Thom Tillis told CBS News on Tuesday night that Hegseth has “a reckoning” coming and his strained relationship with lawmakers was undermining the Trump administration’s push for a $1.5 trillion defence spending package in Congress. “I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he’s the best person to bring those needs to Congress if he wants something done before the end of this Congress, which is only 60 days away,” Tillis said as the midterm results came in. Democrats have promised to investigate Hegseth and his handling of the Pentagon, and aides say that could include everything from his handling of the Iran war to his purges of top military officers including the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. He could also face scrutiny over his Ukraine policy and US military strikes on suspected drug trafficking boats in Latin American waters, which some Democrats say could amount to war crimes. At times, the conflict between Hegseth and members of Congress has become personal. Last year, Hegseth sought to prosecute Democratic US Senator Mark Kelly after he and five other Democrats in Congress with backgrounds in the military and intelligence urged US troops to refuse illegal orders. Hegseth accused them of sedition. Representative Adam Smith, the Democrat who is expected to lead the House Armed Services Committee next year, promised vigorous oversight on everything from the Iran war to what he called the erosion of the “apolitical foundation of the armed forces”. A source familiar with the matter said rancour on Capitol Hill over Hegseth has featured in White House discussions about potential replacements for him, saying there would be a need to have someone in the job who could distance themselves from events under Democratic scrutiny. Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said Hegseth would continue to drive Trump’s agenda and that the Pentagon “has followed the law”. “Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists,” Parnell said. Tennessee Senate seat? One long-rumoured possibility for Hegseth would be filling the Senate seat that will be vacated by Senator Marsha Blackburn, who was elected on Tuesday to become Tennessee’s next governor starting in January. She has four years left in her term, and Hegseth, a Tennessee resident who voted there on Tuesday, could be appointed to the position, without having to run for election. Asked whether he wanted Hegseth to fill Blackburn’s seat, Trump said: “Well, I think, I think he’s doing a very good job, and I actually think he’d be very popular if he did that.” “But I haven’t heard that at all,” Trump told reporters. Trump has regularly praised Hegseth publicly, and has given the former Army National Guard soldier significant leeway as he sought to reshape the Pentagon. But last month Trump publicly split with Hegseth by pulling the plug on his plans to livestream the Army’s firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan.

PTA dismisses 'fake and misleading' notification claiming TikTok banned in Pakistan. The Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) on Thursday dismissed reports of a ban on video-sharing platform TikTok as “false and misleading”, clarifying that no notification to that effect had been issued. In a post on social media platform X, the authority said that a fake notification regarding an alleged ban on TikTok was being circulated on social media. “PTA clarifies that no such notification has been issued, and the circulating information is false and misleading,” it said. The authority advised the public not to share or rely on unverified information. “Citizens should obtain authentic information only through PTA’s official website and verified social media platforms,” the statement said. TikTok has repeatedly been banned in Pakistan in the past over complaints about indecent and immoral content. The first such ban came in October 2020, but was lifted 10 days later, after the company assured the telecom regulator that it would block accounts “spreading obscenity”. In March 2021, the PHC also imposed a ban on the video-​sharing application that was later lifted in April. In June that year, the Sindh High Court had followed suit and ordered the PTA to suspend access to TikTok in the country for “spreading immorality and obscenity”. The court had lifted the suspension three days after issuing the order. But the PTA had again blocked access to the platform in July for its failure to take down “inappropriate content”. The very next month, the Islamabad High Court (IHC) had questioned the PTA’s powers to impose a blanket ban on TikTok, stating that by the same logic, the telecommunication authority should also ban other digital platforms like Google and YouTube. The court had directed the PTA to consult the government and formulate a mechanism to deal with such matters. Eventually, the PTA had lifted the ban in November 2021 following assurances by TikTok that it would “control” the uploading and dissemination of “immoral and indecent content” on the app.

France braces for demonstrations as trade unions strike. Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to take to the streets across France on Thursday, as unions hold strikes alongside student-led demonstrations that have gripped the country for weeks. The high school student movement that began with youth protesting dismal learning conditions has coincided with widespread anger over the rising cost of living and inequality, which culminated on October 17 in the worst rioting France has seen in years. On Thursday, authorities estimate some 500,000 to 700,000 people will protest across the country, while as many as 80,000 people are expected to march in the capital Paris. “It’s going to be a strong mobilisation,” said Marylise Leon of the CFDT union, anticipating a turnout comparable to France’s pension reform protests in 2023 that saw over one million people march. Public and private education unions have called for strike action, as well as unions representing rail workers, public hospitals and postal services. In demands addressed to both the government and employers, the unions are calling for an increase in the minimum wage, which has not received any discretionary boost since 2012, across-the-board wage raises, tax reforms and better learning conditions for young people. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez announced Wednesday that 70,000 police officers and security forces would be deployed across the country, promising “an extremely firm response” to any “acts of violence” or disorder. ‘Wake-up call’ Although student-led protests were largely peaceful, some saw clashes with police erupt with tear gas and water cannon fired to disperse crowds. An attempted murder investigation has been launched after petrol bombs were thrown at security forces in Paris on Saturday. Meanwhile, the police response has been criticised as heavy-handed and internal police investigations have been launched over allegations of brutality against demonstrators. Several teenage protesters have been seriously wounded and thousands arrested. Authorities have admitted to security and intelligence failures that paved the way for the clashes, large-scale looting and vandalism of public property that erupted on October 17. On Wednesday, the Paris prefecture banned a major protest route planned between Place de la Bastille and Place de la Concorde, which would have crossed the centre of the city. Police instead replaced it with an authorised route moving eastward away from the centre. Several unions have denounced route bans as a move to repress freedom of demonstration, and some have filed last-minute appeals to have the routes reinstated. “We can feel a cumulative effect: public sympathy for the high school and university students’ movement is not waning, and people are questioning restrictions on liberties, especially bans on demonstrations,” Fabrice Fort of the CGT union explained. “This has sparked a wake-up call among people who usually don’t speak out much,” he added. Similar protests have sparked in other European countries in recent weeks with youth-led demonstrations seen in Denmark, Germany and Italy.
